key_insight: This study audits the mental health interventions 41 language models recommend when identical clinical information comes from a clinician, caregiver, or patient. The provided abstract describes the audit but does not report whether recommendations differed across these perspectives.
problem_solved: How can we systematically assess whether AI mental health recommendations change depending on who asks, even when the underlying clinical facts stay the same?
method: Presented 41 language models with 19 clinical case vignettes and five questions, framed from clinician, caregiver, and patient perspectives.
Collected 35,055 free-text responses and extracted every named intervention using a validated judge.
Asked 29 models to rate the full list of intervention options.
impact: The audit offers AI/ML practitioners a framework for evaluating role-sensitive behavior in high-stakes mental health advice. It can support safety testing, but the provided abstract does not establish recommendation quality or clinical effectiveness.
visual_elements: Three role icons—clinician, caregiver, and patient—feeding the same clinical case into an AI model.
Audit pipeline: case vignettes → model responses → intervention extraction → option ratings.
Scale badges: 41 models, 19 vignettes, five questions, and 35,055 responses.
Comparison-matrix template showing interventions by user role, without implying unreported differences.
paper_title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
paper_authors: Matthew Flathers, Jill Noorily, Phuong Anh Nguyen, Mark Kalinich, Mina Fallah
